name: Selenium
summary: Selenium is a trace mineral the body builds into a few dozen proteins (selenoproteins), including antioxidant enzymes and the enzymes that activate thyroid hormone. How much is in food depends on the soil it grew in. The gap between enough and too much is narrow, and trials of supplements in people who weren't short didn't prevent cancer or heart disease.
roles: Part of antioxidant enzymes (glutathione peroxidases) that protect cells from damage

status.note: The usual test is plasma or serum selenium. It reflects recent intake and depends on the form eaten (selenomethionine raises it more, because it is stored in body proteins). Selenoprotein P and the enzyme glutathione peroxidase show whether the body has enough to make its selenium proteins, but they stop rising once intake is adequate, so they can't show excess. EFSA based its adequate intake on the point where selenoprotein P levels off. Hair and toenail selenium reflect longer-term intake but are mostly used in research. Selenium isn't usually tested without a reason, and this app has no selenium marker yet.

signs: Clear deficiency is rare in Europe
Heart muscle disease in children and young women in very low-selenium areas of China (Keshan disease)
A joint and bone disease in some low-selenium regions (Kashin-Beck disease)
Muscle pain and weakness in people on long-term drip feeding without added selenium
Possibly weaker immune defences and thyroid problems when intake is low
atRisk: People in regions with low-selenium soil (parts of Europe and China) who eat mostly local food
People with severe gut conditions that limit absorption, such as Crohn's disease or short bowel
Strict vegans in low-selenium areas, since meat, fish and eggs are main sources there

high.note: Too much selenium causes selenosis. Hair loss is one of the first signs, and EFSA based its upper limit on it: in the SELECT trial, men given 200 µg of selenium a day on top of their usual diet (about 330 µg in total) had more hair loss and skin inflammation. EFSA found that adults are unlikely to go over the limit except regular users of high-dose supplements or regular eaters of Brazil nuts.

examples: Brazil nuts (very high and very variable)
Fish and seafood: tuna, sardines, prawns, mussels
Offal such as kidney and liver
Bread and cereals, mushrooms and pulses (amounts depend on the soil)
foodSources.note: Selenium in plant foods depends on the soil they grew in, so the same food can hold very different amounts in different countries. Soils in much of Europe are lower in selenium than in North America.

forms.name: L-selenomethionine (organic)
forms.note: The main form in food. The body can build it into proteins in place of the amino acid methionine, so it raises blood levels more and is stored. SELECT used it.

forms.name: Selenium yeast
forms.note: Yeast grown in a selenium-rich medium; most of its selenium is selenomethionine, with other compounds that vary by product.

forms.name: Sodium selenite and sodium selenate (inorganic)
forms.note: Used directly to make selenoproteins and not stored in body proteins, so they raise blood selenium less than selenomethionine at the same amount. Used in some thyroid trials and in drip feeding.

forms.name: Multivitamins and combination products
forms.note: Many contain selenium, so amounts add up with single supplements and Brazil nuts.

upperLimit.note: Tolerable upper intake level (UL) a day from all food and supplements, for adult men and women including pregnancy and breastfeeding. EFSA set it in 2023, based on hair loss: harm was seen at 330 µg a day in the SELECT trial, and EFSA divided this by a safety factor of 1.3. The intake values are adequate intakes (AI): EFSA couldn't work out an average need, so it used the intake at which selenoprotein P levels off. They are guides for groups, not personal targets.

interactions.with: Type 2 diabetes, or a higher risk of it
interactions.note: Trials raised a possible higher risk of type 2 diabetes with selenium supplements in people who already got enough. Discuss any selenium supplement with your doctor.

interactions.with: Brazil nuts, multivitamins and other selenium sources
interactions.note: Amounts add up. Brazil nuts can contain a lot of selenium, and EFSA names regular Brazil nut eaters and high-dose supplement users as the adults most likely to go over the upper limit.

Selenium is needed to activate thyroid hormone, and specialists sometimes use it for mild Graves' eye disease. For other thyroid conditions the evidence is unclear. Ask the doctor treating your thyroid.

cautions: The gap between the adequate intake (70 µg) and the upper limit (255 µg) is narrow compared with most nutrients.
Brazil nuts vary a lot in selenium depending on where they grew.
Hair loss, brittle nails or a garlic smell on the breath can be signs of too much selenium; these need a doctor.
Trials showing no benefit were mostly in men who already got enough selenium; less is known about people with low intake.

commonUses: May support thyroid health, because selenium is needed to activate thyroid hormone.
May support the immune system's defence against infection.
May act as an antioxidant through selenium-containing enzymes that protect cells from damage.
May support fertility, in both men and women.

origin: Selenium is a trace mineral that the body builds into about two dozen proteins called selenoproteins, including antioxidant enzymes and enzymes that activate thyroid hormone. The body cannot make it. Food gets its selenium from the soil, so the same food can hold very different amounts in different regions.

Supplement selenium is usually made as selenomethionine (the form found in food), selenium yeast grown in a selenium-rich medium, or the inorganic salts sodium selenite and sodium selenate. Many multivitamins also contain it.
dosage: The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) sets an adequate intake (AI) of 70 µg a day for adults and in pregnancy, and 85 µg when breastfeeding. In 2023 EFSA set a tolerable upper intake level (UL, the most that is likely safe every day from food and supplements together) of 255 µg a day for adults, including pregnancy and breastfeeding. The gap between the two is narrow. These are population values, not personal targets.

An amount commonly used in studies and supplements is about 100 to 200 µg a day (200 µg a day in the large cancer and diabetes trials; 100 µg twice a day in a thyroid eye disease trial). This is not a reference intake or a personal recommendation.

When checking a label, look at the form (selenomethionine, selenium yeast, sodium selenite or selenate) and the amount of elemental selenium in one serving, since the compound's weight is larger. Selenomethionine raises blood levels more than selenite. Amounts add up with multivitamins and Brazil nuts, which can contain a lot. Hair loss, brittle nails or a garlic smell on the breath can be signs of too much. People with type 2 diabetes or a higher risk of it, or a thyroid condition, should talk to their doctor before using selenium supplements.

foodAmounts.verdict: Yes. The adequate intake can be reached from ordinary food, especially fish, seafood, eggs and meat. Brazil nuts are a special case: their selenium content varies a lot with the soil they grew in, so a table value is only a rough guide, and a few nuts can bring a person near or over the upper limit. Plant foods also vary with local soil. For example, for the EFSA adequate intake, adults, about 30 g of brazil nuts, or about 80 g of canned tuna, drained; for the amount commonly used in studies, about 80 g of brazil nuts, or about 230 g of canned tuna, drained.
foodAmounts.notChecked: Food values are from the UK food composition table (McCance and Widdowson's CoFID 2021) built into this app, for the food named. Cooked, stored or processed foods and other brands differ. These are amounts eaten, not absorbed.
